content: Chenopodium is a genus comprising approximately 150 species of herbaceous flowering plants, either annual or perennial, commonly referred to as goosefoots. These plants are distributed globally and are classified under the family Amaranthaceae according to the APG II system. Historically, they were placed in a separate family, Chenopodiaceae, but this classification rendered the remaining Amaranthaceae polyphyletic. Within the Amaranthaceae family, Chenopodium is the representative genus of the subfamily Chenopodioideae. The genus Dysphania is closely related to Chenopodium and includes species previously classified under Chenopodium, such as epazote (Dysphania ambrosioides). In Australia, larger Chenopodium species are colloquially known as blue bushes. The town of Chualar in California derives its name from a Native American term for a goosefoot species abundant in the area, likely the California goosefoot (Chenopodium californicum). Several species within the Chenopodium genus are of minor to moderate importance as food crops. These plants are utilized as leafy vegetables, similar to spinach (Spinacia oleracea), and as pseudocereals. Examples include white goosefoot (Chenopodium album), Good King Henry (Chenopodium bonus-henricus), strawberry blite (Chenopodium capitatum), leafy goosefoot (Chenopodium foliosum), kañiwa (Chenopodium pallidicaule), and quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa). On the Greek island of Crete, tender shoots and leaves of a local species, known as krouvida (κρουβίδα) or psaroblito (ψαρόβλητο), are consumed after boiling or steaming. Archaeological studies, such as those by Kristen Gremillion, indicate that goosefoots have been used as food since at least 4000 BC. For instance, pitseed goosefoot (Chenopodium berlandieri) was a staple crop in the Native American Eastern Agricultural Complex, while white goosefoot was utilized by the Ertebølle culture in Europe. Today, there is growing interest in goosefoot seeds, particularly for their suitability in gluten-free diets. Quinoa oil, extracted from Chenopodium quinoa seeds, is of higher quality than corn oil. Additionally, oil from epazote seeds, now classified outside the Chenopodium genus, was historically used. Goosefoot seeds were also employed in the past to produce shagreen leather. Chenopodium album has been a key model organism for molecular biological studies, particularly in the investigation of chlorophyllase. However, pollen from goosefoot species, especially the widespread Chenopodium album, is a common allergen and a significant cause of hay fever. Some species produce seeds capable of persisting in the soil seed bank for years, contributing to their status as notable weeds. Certain species have become invasive, forming dense thickets that provide cover for small animals. Goosefoot foliage serves as a food source for caterpillars of specific Lepidoptera species, while the seeds are consumed by various birds, such as the yellowhammer (Emberiza citrinella) in Europe and the white-winged fairy-wren (Malurus leucopterus) in Australia. Pathogens affecting goosefoot species include positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses like the apple stem grooving virus, sowbane mosaic virus, and tobacco necrosis virus. The genus Chenopodium includes numerous species, such as Chenopodium album (white goosefoot), Chenopodium bonus-henricus (Good King Henry), Chenopodium capitatum (strawberry blite), Chenopodium pallidicaule (kañiwa), and Chenopodium quinoa (quinoa). Other notable species include Chenopodium berlandieri (pitseed goosefoot), Chenopodium californicum (California goosefoot), and Chenopodium rubrum (red goosefoot). Some species formerly classified under Chenopodium, such as Dysphania botrys and Rhagodia baccata, have been reclassified into other genera.
